To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the active sites for alkane isomerization on tungstated zirconias are Zr-WO(3-x) species, and (ii) the number density of these species can be increased by two orders-of-magnitude by a simple synthesis procedure.

the active sites for light alkane isomerization on tungstated zirconias consist of subnanometre clusters of Zr-WOx, which have a higher density of active sites than larger clusters or WO3 particles, and can be generated by a synthesis route that deliberately increases the density of these subnanometre species.

high-angle annular darkfield imaging in an aberration corrected electron microscope allows the direct imaging of the active sites in tungstated zirconium oxide catalysts, that these active sites are Zr-WOx clusters, and that the number density of these clusters is the key parameter that determines the activity of the catalyst.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new catalysts for light alkane isomerization, the identification of the active site in these catalysts and the development of methods to synthesize these catalysts.
the development of new solid acid catalysts for the isomerization of light alkanes.
the synthesis, characterization and application of novel materials, with a particular focus on catalysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the active site is a small Zr-WO3 cluster, with a Zr/W ratio of approximately 3, which can be prepared by a solvothermal method.
WO(x) clusters of 1-2 nm in diameter on ZrO2 are the most active species in the isomerization of light alkanes.
Zr-WO3 clusters of less than 2 nm in size are responsible for the isomerization of alkanes on the ZrO2-WOx catalyst.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified the active site in the catalyst, and we have used that information to design new catalysts with improved performance.

the combination of advanced synthesis methods, advanced characterization tools (including aberration-correcting analytical electron microscopy) and theoretical calculations can be used to design and understand solid acid catalysts.

we have used aberration-correcting transmission electron microscopy to directly image the active sites on a solid acid catalyst and have used that information to improve the activity of the material by more than an order of magnitude.
The main takeaway from our work is that
high-angle annular darkfield imaging is a powerful tool for the direct structural imaging of active species in supported metal oxide catalysts.
the catalytic activity of a solid acid is directly related to the number density of subnanometre active sites, and not to their size.
the use of high-resolution analytical imaging can provide direct evidence for the identity of the catalytically active species, which can then be used to guide further catalyst development.
